articles.title: Coexistence of Ebstein Anomaly and Cerebral Cavernous Malformation: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: In most patients who have Ebstein anomaly (EA), neurological symptoms are either associated with thromboembolic episodes or due to arrhythmic complications. Cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) is a vascular anomaly made up of sinusoidally dilated blood vessels, often presenting with seizure activity or intracranial bleeding. There has never been any documented report regarding coexisting EA and CCM. Herein, we have reported a 32-year-old female with an established history of Ebstein anomaly diagnosed in 2013 who had a history of generalized tonic-clonic fits since 2020. Neuroimaging studies showed the presence of a right frontal lobe mass with typical "popcorn-like" appearance and hemosiderin ring on MRI, indicative of cerebral cavernous malformation. The patient declined surgery and was managed conservatively with levetiracetam. With the occurrence of further fits in 2025, neuroimaging showed similar findings but without the presence of intratumoral bleeding. Subsequently, she underwent a left frontoparietal craniotomy for GTE of the lesion with cavernoma on histopathology. The neurological status of the patient was stable during her discharge on the fourth postoperative day. This case documents a previously unreported coexistence of Ebstein anomaly and cerebral cavernous malformation in a single patient. Given the rarity of both conditions, coexistence is coincidental. This indicates the need for genetic and molecular studies to determine whether a real biological association exists.

articles.title: Musculoskeletal Histopathology of Klippel-Trénaunay Syndrome: A Clinicopathologic Study of 21 Cases With Long-Term Orthopedic Follow-Up.
articles.abstract: Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome (KTS) is a rare congenital vascular-overgrowth disorder within the broader spectrum of PIK3CA-related overgrowth syndromes. Although clinical, radiologic, and orthopedic manifestations are well described, the histologic spectrum of KTS-associated pathology remains under-characterized. Clinicopathologic findings from 21 patients with clinically established KTS were reviewed, including 18 with longitudinal clinical follow-up and 3 consultation cases of rare malignant mesenchymal neoplasms. Cases were identified from institutional pathology and clinical databases, and available hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections and ancillary studies were reviewed. The cohort included 11 males and 10 females. Among the 18 clinically followed patients, 12 had limb length discrepancy or asymmetric limb overgrowth, 9 had documented deep vascular malformations, 4 had intra-articular/synovial malformations, and 10 underwent initial orthopedic evaluation or intervention before age 18. Orthopedic morbidity clustered into mechanical overgrowth-related, vascular malformation-related, and soft tissue/wound-related complications. Histologic findings included superficial and/or deep slow-flow vascular malformations, ulceration and granulation tissue, hemosiderin-laden reactive synovium, and destructive hemorrhagic arthropathy. Intra-articular disease recapitulated a hemophilic arthropathy-like pattern, with hemosiderotic synovitis, papillary synovial hyperplasia, and progressive joint destruction with loss of articular cartilage, exposed subchondral bone destruction and remodeling, all attributable to long-standing intra-articular hemorrhage. Three consultation cases showed malignant mesenchymal neoplasia, including 2 angiosarcomas. Recognition of these patterns is important for pathologists evaluating specimens from patients with known or suspected KTS, particularly when findings mimic hemophilic arthropathy, diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor, nonsyndromic vascular malformation, and/or end-stage destructive arthropathy.

articles.title: Delayed diagnosis of a traumatic gluteal pseudoaneurysm with arteriovenous fistula and dual arterial supply mimicking a buttock abscess after a stab wound: a case report.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traumatic arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs), with or without associated pseudoaneurysms, are uncommon complications of penetrating vascular injuries that may cause substantial morbidity and potentially fatal complications. Evidence is largely derived from case reports and case series, with important contributions from military experience. Delayed gluteal lesions may mimic a hematoma or abscess, creating a diagnostic pitfall.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 51-year-old male presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging painful left buttock mass following a stab wound that had been primarily sutured at a local hospital. Initial ultrasound suggested a hematoma, and the patient was admitted with a working diagnosis of "left buttock mass." Physical examination revealed a 7 × 7 cm fluctuant mass with tenderness but without overt signs of infection. Contrast-enhanced pelvic CT demonstrated a 6.8 × 3.2 cm intensely enhancing lesion within the left gluteus maximus with prominent feeding vessels, suggestive of an arteriovenous fistula or vascular malformation. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed a left gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated arteriovenous fistula supplied by branches of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries, with early venous opacification. The patient underwent successful transcatheter embolization using fibered platinum coils and a cyanoacrylate-lipiodol mixture, with complete occlusion of the fistula confirmed on completion angiography. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 2. At three-month follow-up, the patient reported no specific discomfort, and color Doppler ultrasonography showed a marked reduction in mass size with no detectable flow within the lesion.
CONCLUSION: Penetrating buttock trauma may cause a gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated AVF supplied by more than one internal iliac artery branch. Contrast-enhanced CT and selective angiography are important for recognizing the vascular lesion and delineating all feeding arteries. In this patient, embolization of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arterial feeders achieved complete angiographic occlusion and a favorable clinical outcome, with a markedly smaller mass and no detectable intralesional flow on color Doppler ultrasonography at three months.

articles.title: Endothelial fluid shear stress sensing in vascular health and disease.
articles.abstract: Endothelial cells transduce the frictional force from blood flow (fluid shear stress) into biochemical signals that regulate gene expression and cell behavior via specialized mechanisms and pathways. These pathways shape the vascular system during development and during postnatal and adult life to optimize flow to tissues. The same pathways also contribute to atherosclerosis and vascular malformations. This Review covers recent advances in basic mechanisms of flow signaling and the involvement of these mechanisms in vascular physiology, remodeling, and these diseases. We propose that flow sensing pathways that govern normal morphogenesis can contribute to disease under pathological conditions or can be altered to induce disease. Viewing atherosclerosis and vascular malformations as instances of pathological morphogenesis provides a unifying perspective that may aid in developing new therapies.

articles.title: Nonconventional Use of Flash-Lamp Pulsed-Dye Laser in Dermatology.
articles.abstract: Flash-lamp pulsed-dye laser (FPDL) is a nonablative technology, typically used in vascular malformation therapy due to its specificity for hemoglobin. FPDL treatments were performed in a large group of patients with persistent and/or recalcitrant different dermatological lesions with cutaneous microvessel involvement. In particular, 149 patients (73 males and 76 females) were treated. They were affected by the following dermatological disorders: angiokeratoma circumscriptum, genital and extragenital viral warts, striae rubrae, basal cell carcinoma, Kaposi's sarcoma, angiolymphoid hyperplasia, and Jessner-Kanof disease. They all underwent various laser sessions. 89 patients (59.7%) achieved excellent clearance, 32 patients (21.4%) achieved good-moderate clearance, 19 patients (12.7%) obtained slight clearance, and 9 subjects (6.1%) had low or no removal of their lesion. In all cases, FPDL was found to be a safe and effective treatment for the abovementioned dermatological lesions in which skin microvessels play a role in pathogenesis or development. Further and single-indication studies, however, are required to assess a standardized and reproducible method for applying this technology to "off-label" indications.

articles.title: Sociodemographic variation in 30-day outcomes after pediatric arteriovenous malformation resection: A national surgical quality improvement program-pediatric analysis, 2016-2024.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pediatric cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM) care shows documented disparities in access to high-volume centers, yet it is unknown whether sociodemographic factors predict validated perioperative outcomes among children who undergo resection.
METHODS: The American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program-Pediatric identified 1558 AVM resections (Current Procedural Terminology codes 61680-61692) during 2016-2024. The primary exposure was race and ethnicity; the primary outcome was 30-day composite morbidity. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, transfer route, acuity, American Society of Anesthesiologists class, lesion location and complexity, comorbidities, hemorrhagic presentation, and operative year. Firth penalization, an E-value, causal mediation, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and sensitivity analyses were applied. Probabilistic bias analysis addressed rupture misclassification, bounding analyses addressed unreported race, and a major-morbidity composite addressed outcome heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Composite morbidity occurred in 143 children (9.2%). Non-Hispanic (NH) Black children had higher adjusted odds than NH White children (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.03, 95% CI 1.17-3.50; p = 0.011); no other group differed. Adjusted morbidity probability was 14.6% versus 7.9% (risk difference +6.6 %age points). The estimate was identical under Firth penalization; the E-value was 3.17. Presentation acuity did not mediate the association (indirect-effect OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.97-1.03), and hemorrhagic presentation did not differ by race (p = 0.291). The estimate remained near 2.0 under simulated true rupture prevalences of 50-70% and strengthened for a major-morbidity composite (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.18-3.81). Prolonged length of stay and nonroutine discharge were directionally concordant but not significant after FDR correction.
CONCLUSIONS: NH Black children exhibited increased adjusted odds of 30-day morbidity after AVM resection, independent of presentation acuity and clinical severity. Because NSQIP-P records no facility identifier, differential access to high-volume centers remains the most plausible unmeasured explanation, and this association should be read as a signal warranting center-level investigation rather than as evidence of race-specific perioperative risk. These findings complement documented access disparities and support validated-outcome surveillance in pediatric AVM care.

articles.title: Mimic of Peritoneal Carcinomatosis: Protein-Losing Enteropathy Revealing HRAS-Driven Generalized Lymphatic Anomaly.
articles.abstract: Complex lymphatic anomalies can present with a protein-losing enteropathy. A 25-year-old woman presented with steatorrhea, weight loss, anasarca, and hypoalbuminemia. Abdominal computed tomography revealed diffuse peritoneal soft tissue lesions concerning for carcinomatosis. Omental biopsies and magnetic resonance lymphangiography established generalized lymphatic anomaly. Targeted genetic sequencing identified a novel postzygotic HRAS insertion mutation. She was started on a low-fat diet, sirolimus, and trametinib monotherapy with modest symptomatic response. However, she continued to have severe malnutrition. Alternating therapy of sirolimus and trametinib is ongoing. This is the first reported case of protein-losing enteropathy as the presenting manifestation of an HRAS-driven generalized lymphatic anomaly.

articles.title: Vascular anomalies: classification, imaging characteristics and implications for interventional radiology treatment approaches.
articles.abstract: The term vascular anomaly represents a broad spectrum of vascular pathology, including proliferating vascular tumours and vascular malformations. While the treatment of most vascular anomalies is multifactorial, interventional radiology procedures, including embolic therapy, sclerotherapy and laser coagulation among others, are playing an increasingly important role in vascular anomaly management. This review discusses the diagnosis and treatment of common vascular malformations, with emphasis on the technique, efficacy and complications of different interventional radiology procedures.

articles.title: Propranolol therapy for reducing the number of nasal infantile hemangioma invasive procedures.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Propranolol therapy is changing the treatment paradigm for infantile hemangioma. This study addresses the effect of propranolol therapy on the treatment of nasal infantile hemangioma (NIH), an area that often does not respond to medical therapy.
OBJECTIVE: To determine if propranolol treatment is associated with fewer invasive treatments for NIH.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Retrospective cohort study conducted within a single pediatric institution's multidisciplinary vascular anomaly program for patients with NIH treated between January 1, 2003, and December 31, 2011. Three NIH cohorts were compared: prepropranolol (20 in group 1; 2003-2009), propranolol (25 in group 2; 2009-2011), and nonpropranolol (13 in group 3; 2009-2011) treatment.
INTERVENTIONS: Analysis of systemic medical, laser, or surgical therapies for NIH.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The study plan was created to detect a change in invasive therapy for NIH. Data collected included presenting age, sex, affected nasal subunits, infantile hemangioma morphologic characteristics, treatment type and number, and primary treating service. An NIH grading system, based on nasal subunit involvement, helped quantify treatment change. Descriptive statistics summarized data, and a Cox proportional hazards regression model evaluated propranolol use and the likelihood of invasive treatments (surgical excision or laser).
RESULTS: Of the 95 patients identified, 58 met inclusion criteria: 20 in group 1 (mean age, 4.8 months), 25 in group 2 (mean age, 4.9 months), and 13 in group 3 (mean age, 4.9 months). Nasal infantile hemangiomas involved the nasal tip subunit in 33 of 58 patients (56.9%). Eight of 13 patients (61.5%) in group 3 frequently had small NIH (grade 1). Patients in group 2 were less likely to undergo any invasive treatments (relative risk, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.73), have surgical excision only (0.45; 0.15-1.38), or undergo laser treatment only (0.44; 0.27-0.78) compared with those in group 1. Patients with higher-grade NIH had more medical or invasive therapy, but invasive procedures were carried out in each subgroup defined by grade.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Patients with isolated propranolol-treated NIH were less likely to undergo invasive treatment, but despite its implementation, the need for invasive treatment was not totally supplanted by its use.

articles.title: Focal malformations of cortical development: new vistas for molecular pathogenesis.
articles.abstract: Focal malformations of cortical development (FMCD) are highly associated with several neurological disorders including intractable epilepsy and neurocognitive disabilities. Over the past decade, several FMCD subtypes have been linked to hyperactivation of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling cascade. In view of the roles that mTOR plays in cell proliferation, size, motility, and stem cell phenotype, many of the features of FMCD such as cytomegaly, disorganized lamination, and expression of stem cell markers can be explained by enhanced mTOR signaling. FMCD result from several distinct and fascinating molecular mechanisms including biallelic gene inactivation, somatic mutation, and potentially, viral infection. These mechanisms have been directly linked to mTOR activation. Perhaps most compelling, pharmacological inhibition of mTOR has been implemented successfully in clinical trials for select FMCD and provides a new vista for treatment.

articles.title: The Impact of Plasmapheresis on Serum Concentrations of Antiseizure Medications: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Seizures are an important neurological manifestation of several autoimmune and antibody-mediated disorders and often require treatment with antiseizure medications (ASMs). Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is frequently used to treat these antibody-mediated conditions by removing circulating pathogenic factors. However, TPE is non-selective and may also remove protein-bound ASMs, particularly those with low volume of distribution. This unintended drug clearance may result in subtherapeutic concentrations and breakthrough seizures. This study aims to systematically assess the available evidence on the effects of TPE on ASM serum concentrations. It also seeks to determine whether drug removal is clinically significant and needs post-procedure supplemental dosing. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library from April to May 2025 using predefined MeSH terms and keywords related to epilepsy, ASMs, and TPE. Randomized trials and case reports/series involving patients receiving ASMs concomitantly with TPE and reporting serum drug concentrations were included. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. The primary outcome was the effect of TPE on ASM serum concentrations and the need for dose adjustment. Eighteen studies comprising 30 patients were included. Phenytoin was the most frequently evaluated ASM; although total serum concentrations often declined during TPE, overall drug removal was generally low, and free levels frequently remained therapeutic. Phenobarbital showed minimal change, while valproate and several newer ASMs demonstrated variable reductions in serum concentrations. Breakthrough seizures were reported in seven studies, ranging from transient events to refractory seizures requiring dose adjustments or treatment discontinuation. The effect of TPE on ASM pharmacokinetics was found to be drug-specific and largely influenced by protein binding and volume of distribution. Although overall drug removal is generally limited, peri-procedural serum fluctuations may contribute to breakthrough seizures in vulnerable patients. Routine supplemental dosing is not generally recommended; instead, individualized monitoring, and post-session dosing strategies are advised, particularly for ASMs with low volume of distribution or in high-risk patients.

articles.title: Case Report: Efgartigimod in refractory non-tumor Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
articles.abstract: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a rare autoimmune disorder, associated with neoplastic disease in 50-60% of cases. In severe cases, currently available immunomodulatory therapies frequently fail to achieve adequate control. We report a 20-year-old woman with non-tumor LEMS refractory to 3,4-diaminopyridine, sequential immunosuppression with prednisone, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and rituximab and plasma exchange, who remained severely disabled after two years of progressive disease. Off-label efgartigimod (1000mg subcutaneously weekly for four weeks, with the interval between cycles initially adjusted according to symptom recurrence), produced rapid and sustained clinical improvement, including recovery from a respiratory decompensation episode. The Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) score decreased from a baseline of 5-9 to a minimum of 2, and the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) score improved from 13-18 to 8-11. Symptoms consistently recurred toward the end of the third week of each treatment-free interval, prompting a fixed two-week interval, which stabilized clinical response and reduced fluctuation severity. This is, to our knowledge, the first report of sustained clinical benefit from FcRn inhibition in non-paraneoplastic, long-standing refractory LEMS. As in myasthenia gravis, LEMS is mediated by pathogenic circulating IgG antibodies, and these findings support FcRn inhibition as a rational treatment strategy in refractory LEMS regardless of tumor association.

articles.title: Anti-GBM disease shortly after clinically presumed ANCA-associated vasculitis in an 85-year-old patient: a case report and literature review.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sequential emergence of anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease after anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is rare.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 85-year-old woman presented with fever, edema, elevated myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA, mild urinary abnormalities, markedly elevated urinary tubular injury markers, and negative serum anti-GBM antibodies measured by chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay. Renal biopsy was not performed because of advanced age, severe dementia, antiplatelet therapy, and the family's preference for non-invasive management. She was clinically presumed to have AAV and achieved apparent clinical remission with prednisolone alone, although MPO-ANCA remained positive. However, 2.5 months after the initial AAV diagnosis, she developed rapidly progressive kidney failure requiring dialysis, accompanied by severe hematuria, increased proteinuria, urinary casts, and markedly elevated anti-GBM antibodies. Clinically diagnosed anti-GBM disease was treated with methylprednisolone pulse therapy, prednisolone, plasma exchange, and hemodialysis. Although renal recovery was not achieved, anti-GBM antibodies became negative, and she remained clinically stable on maintenance hemodialysis for over 4 years while receiving low-dose prednisolone.
CONCLUSION: This case suggests that anti-GBM disease can emerge shortly after apparent clinical remission of AAV. ANCA-mediated GBM injury and age-related GBM changes may contribute to subsequent anti-GBM autoimmunity, although these mechanisms remain hypothetical in this patient. Prompt anti-GBM antibody testing should be considered when a rapid, unexplained decline in kidney function occurs during or after AAV treatment.

articles.title: ANCA-associated vasculitis in the United Arab Emirates: a 17-year case series with review from Gulf literature.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a rare and severe autoimmune disease characterized by pauci-immune necrotizing vasculitis.
OBJECTIVES: The study aims to explore the frequency, clinical characteristics, and management of AAV patients in two tertiary centers in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) over 17 years.
DESIGN: A retrospective observational case series.
SETTING: Two tertiary centers in the UAE.
METHODS: Patients diagnosed with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) from 2008 to 2024 were included. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, histopathological information, treatment, complications, relapses, and mortality were collected. ANCA testing for anti-proteinase 3 (PR3) and anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) antibodies was performed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed to summarize the data.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Subtype distribution, organ involvement, ANCA positivity, relapse, and mortality rates.
SAMPLE SIZE: Twenty-six patients.
RESULTS: We identified 26 AAV patients with a median age of 52.5 years. The majority were females (58%, n=15), and half were locals. The most common AAV subtype was microscopic polyangiitis (50%, n=13), followed by granulomatosis with polyangiitis (38%, n=10) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (12%, n=3). ANCAs tested positive in nearly all of these cases. The most common clinical manifestations of AAV were constitutional symptoms with renal and pulmonary involvement. The induction therapy included corticosteroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, and plasma exchange. The most prescribed maintenance medications were corticosteroids and azathioprine. The overall relapse rate was 31%, and the overall mortality rate was 19% (n=5).
CONCLUSION: In our cohort, MPA was the most common subtype, being predominantly associated with P-ANCA/MPO-ANCA positivity. Notably, few studies from the Gulf region have addressed this topic. It's unclear whether this finding reflects low occurrence or potential underdiagnosis and, thus, points to unmet needs and a significant gap in the understanding of AAV. Multicenter studies are needed to validate these results and improve AAV management in Middle Eastern populations.
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective design with small number of participants.

articles.title: Immunotherapy considerations for distal sensory-predominant and small-fiber peripheral neuropathies.
articles.abstract: Increasing knowledge about the common widespread, distal-predominant polyneuropathies is shifting the standard of care beyond merely palliating symptom toward intervention. This is less advanced for the more prevalent but harder-to-ascertain distal sensory polyneuropathies (DSP) than for motor and demyelinating neuropathies. DSP comprises the sensory-predominant large-fiber axonal/demyelinating neuropathies plus the small-fiber sensory/autonomic axonopathies. Small-fiber disturbances can cause premature fatigue, neuropathic pain and itch, postural orthostasis tachycardia, and gastrointestinal distress. Diagnosis is difficult - screening for classic causes is mandatory but unproductive in a third to a half of patients (initially idiopathic DSP/iiDSP). Multiple large case series and two small passive-transfer studies suggest that autoimmunity may be a prevalent cause of iiDSP, particularly for small-fiber neuropathy. So, despite the knowledge gaps, immunotherapies effective for other neuropathies are increasingly considered for dysimmune iiDSP; particularly in otherwise healthy young patients with impaired life trajectories. To inform these difficult treatment decisions, this chapter summarizes diagnostic requirements for large- and small-fiber iiDSP and evaluates the type and strength of the evidence suggesting autoimmune causality in some. Concomitant rheumatologic conditions including often undiagnosed Sjögren's syndrome, predispose. Youth, abrupt onset, other organ dysimmunity, immune seromarkers, and prior responses to immunotherapy can provide additional evidence, but autoantibody panels are almost never useful. Uncontrolled studies suggest that apparently autoimmune DSP sometimes responds to corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins, and plasmapheresis. However, these cannot be prescribed indiscriminately due to risk, cost/availability, and lack of controlled trials and guidelines. Enough preliminary data may have accrued to permit formulating initial consensus recommendations for selecting the subsets of patients in whom immunotherapy should or should not be considered. Patients, clinicians, and payors would benefit immediately, and highlighting priorities for research could promote long-term advances.

articles.title: Photobiomodulation: multifaceted therapeutic effects on disorders in the central nervous system.
articles.abstract: Conventional pharmacological interventions for brain diseases are often limited by complex pathophysiological mechanisms, suboptimal efficacy, and pronounced side effects. In contrast, photobiomodulation (PBM) has attracted increasing attention due to its non-invasive nature, multi-target effects, and favourable safety profile. In brain diseases, PBM employs specific light wavelengths to activate mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and photosensitive proteins and to regulate neuronal oscillatory activity and neuroglial functions. Human studies demonstrated the efficacy of PBM in improving cognitive performance, motor symptoms, and emotional distress in patients with neurodegenerative diseases, brain trauma, and psychiatric disorders. Therapeutic outcomes are influenced by key parameters of the protocol, such as wavelength, dosage, and frequency, as well as inter-individual variability in anatomical and physiological factors. Future research needs to focus on establishing a database of disease-specific parameters to enable personalised treatment protocols by integrating imaging and molecular biomarkers and performing large-scale clinical trials to validate long-term safety and translational potential.

articles.title: Functional Heterogeneity of the Autism Spectrum Disorder-Associated Gut Microbial Ecosystem Revealed by Fecal Lipopolysaccharides and Bacterial Proteomic Profiling.
articles.abstract: The etiology of pediatric autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been increasingly linked to alterations in the gut-brain axis, highlighting the intricate bidirectional communication between gut microbiota and central nervous system. The molecular mechanisms of this communication are poorly understood. Here we investigated whether ASD-associated gut microbiota could exhibit altered inflammatory molecular outputs by integrating chemistry-driven profiling of fecal lipopolysaccharides (LPS), functional bacterial proteomics, and neuroimmune cellular assays. Structural analyses revealed that LPS from non-autistic healthy donors (NASD) displayed highly conserved carbohydrate and lipid A signatures dominated by hypo-acylated mono-phosphorylated species typically associated with immunomodulatory Bacteroides-derived LPS. In contrast, LPS from ASD children exhibited increased structural heterogeneity. These molecular alterations were functionally reflected in human HMC3 microglial cells, where ASD-derived fecal LPS induced stronger IL-6 and IL-8 release compared with NASD-derived LPS, indicating enhanced neuroinflammatory potential. Functional proteomic profiling disclosed broadly comparable microbial compositions but marked metabolic divergence. These findings suggest that gut microbiota in ASD children are associated with a functionally heterogeneous microbial ecosystem characterized by altered immunostimulatory molecular outputs despite the absence of massive taxonomic shifts, with potential relevance for neuroimmune dysregulation.

articles.title: A rare case of ultrastructurally proven toxoplasmic myositis masquerading as necrotizing myopathy with emphasis on pathobiology.
articles.abstract: Toxoplasmosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the obligate protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. In an immunocompetent human host, the parasite forms bradyzoites (tissue cysts), mainly in skeletal muscle, eye, brain, or cardiac muscle, and remains latent. Once cysts are established, type 1 cytokine-based immunity controls the conversion to tachyzoites from bradyzoites. We propose that short-term immunosuppression can only cause a transient defect in this cycle of conversion control. The temporary lapse in conversion control releases few tachyzoites, and the host immunity in response gives rise to cytokines that can cause polymyositis. Myositis and the presence of a parasite in the muscle biopsy are very rare, even in immunosuppressed patients. We present a case of a young man with quadriplegia after immunosuppression for dengue-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. We report a rare case of toxoplasmic myositis in a patient masquerading as necrotizing myopathy, with emphasis on the possible pathomechanism of myositis and ultrastructure of toxoplasma. We recommend that toxoplasma myositis should be included among the differentials of sudden muscular weakness, especially in an immunocompromised host. Our case highlights the crucial role of muscle biopsy in the diagnosis of toxoplasmic myositis. For early diagnosis, a systematic search for toxoplasmosis should be formulated in case of polymyositis, especially in immunocompromised patients, as a quicker identification of the parasite is possible and treatment response is also better in the early, acute phase of toxoplasmic myositis.

articles.title: Stage-Specific Patterns of Imaging and Non-Motor Biomarkers in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Advancements in disease-modifying therapies for spinocerebellar ataxia Type 3 (SCA3) underscore the need for robust biomarkers to monitor disease progression and evaluate treatment efficacy. Although motor phenotypes have been well characterized, less is known about non-motor and imaging-based features across different disease stages. This study aimed to characterize stage-specific patterns of non-motor and imaging biomarkers in SCA3.
METHODS: This cross-observational study included 229 patients with SCA3 and 104 age- and sex-matched healthy controls from the Organization for Southeast China for cerebellar ataxia research. Non-motor symptoms were assessed using a battery of neuropsychological tests. Brain volume loss was assessed by 3.0-Tesla MRI with regions-of-interest (ROI)-based volumetric analysis. Neuroinflammation was quantified in vivo using translocator protein positron emission tomography (TSPO-PET) with the 18F-DPA-714 radioligand. Additive regression models were fitted to evaluate the cross-sectional associations between biomarkers and disease stages. Receiver operating curve (ROC) analyses were applied to estimate the discriminative ability of the candidate biomarkers.
RESULTS: Non-motor symptoms, including cognitive functions, anxiety, fatigue, depression, and sleep quality, declined after ataxia onset in SCA3. Volume loss in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon diverged from normal controls at 0.7 and 0.2 years before ataxia onset, respectively. Correspondingly, the TSPO signal in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon increased and deviated from normal throughout the disease course.
INTERPRETATION: Our findings propose a staging model of SCA3 that includes a biomarker stage characterized by multidimensional objective indicators of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation from pre-ataxia to ataxia onset.

articles.title: Highly potent, brain-penetrant EP2 receptor antagonists for the treatment of permanent focal cerebral ischaemia in male and female mice.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Cerebral ischaemia is a leading cause of death in older adults and imposes a substantial global economic burden. Recent studies indicate that inhibiting the Gαs-coupled EP2 receptor reduces ischaemic brain injury by modulating neuroinflammation. However, these findings derive from the transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model, which represents only a small subset of large-vessel occlusion (LVO) cases with successful recanalisation.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We characterised the pharmacokinetic parameters of selective EP2 antagonists CJ-18, CJ-19 and CJ-21 that we recently developed. We evaluated their therapeutic efficacy in mice subjected to permanent MCAO (pMCAO), a model that more accurately reflects the majority of LVO cases, and assessed the impact of EP2 inhibition on brain injury and inflammation. Finally, we examined the effects of EP2 inhibition in neuron-glia mixed cultures exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) without reoxygenation.
KEY RESULTS: After systemic administration in mice, new compounds exhibited favourable plasma half-lives and brain penetration. In the pMCAO model, treatment with EP2 antagonists significantly reduced brain infarction in both male and female mice, in a dose-dependent manner, whilst improving sensorimotor performance without affecting muscle strength. These benefits were accompanied by reduced neuronal death, lowered pro-inflammatory cytokines and attenuated reactive gliosis within the ischaemic penumbra. In addition, EP2 inhibition by CJ-18 conferred marked neuroprotection in neuron-glia co-cultures exposed to prolonged OGD, preserving neurite integrity and postsynaptic density.
CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: This proof-of-concept study supports our drug-like EP2 receptor antagonists, particularly CJ-18, as potential treatments for permanent focal cerebral ischaemia.

articles.title: [Effect of electroacupuncture on microglial activation in the spinal dorsal horn of rats with postherpetic neuralgia based on the BDNF/TrkB pathway].
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To observe the effects of electroacupuncture (EA) on the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tyrosine kinase receptor B (TrkB) pathway and microglial activation in the spinal dorsal horn of rats with postherpetic neuralgia (PHN).
METHODS: Five of 20 male SD rats were randomly assigned to the normal control (NC) group, and the remaining rats received intraperitoneal injection of resiniferatoxin solution (200 μg/kg) to establish a PHN model. Successfully modeled rats were randomly divided into a PHN group, an EA group, and an EA+BDNF group, with 5 rats in each group. The rats in the EA group received EA at ashi points, "Xinshu" (BL15), and "Danshu" (BL19) on the left side, with disperse-dense wave (2 Hz/15 Hz) and a current intensity of 1 mA, 30 min per session, once daily for 4 consecutive weeks. In the EA+BDNF group, 10 μg of recombinant rat BDNF protein solution was administered by intrathecal injection before each EA treatment. The mechanical withdrawal threshold was assessed using Von Frey analgesia meter, and the thermal withdrawal latency was evaluated using plantar thermal stimulation apparatus. Immunofluorescence staining was used to detect the positive expression of ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba-1), a marker of microglial activation, in the spinal dorsal horn. ELISA was used to measure interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels in the spinal dorsal horn. Western blot was used to detect the protein expression of BDNF and TrkB in the spinal dorsal horn.
RESULTS: Compared with the NC group, the PHN group showed decreased mechanical withdrawal threshold and increased thermal withdrawal latency (P<0.05), while positive Iba-1 expression, IL-1β and TNF-α levels, and BDNF and TrkB protein expression in the spinal dorsal horn were increased (P<0.05). Compared with the PHN group, the EA group showed increased mechanical withdrawal threshold and decreased thermal withdrawal latency (P<0.05), while positive Iba-1 expression, IL-1β and TNF-α levels, and BDNF and TrkB protein expression in the spinal dorsal horn were decreased (P<0.05). Compared with the EA+BDNF group, the EA group showed increased mechanical withdrawal threshold and decreased thermal withdrawal latency (P<0.05), while positive Iba-1 expression, IL-1β and TNF-α levels, and BDNF and TrkB protein expression in the spinal dorsal horn were all decreased (P<0.05).
CONCLUSION: EA could alleviate pain symptoms in rats with PHN, possibly by regulating the BDNF/TrkB pathway, inhibiting microglial activation in the spinal dorsal horn, and reducing inflammatory factor levels.

articles.title: Blood-brain barrier disruption and microglia-associated synaptic pruning contribute to cognitive decline after electroconvulsive therapy.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Modified electroconvulsive therapy (MECT) is a highly effective intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its broader clinical application is constrained by poorly understood cognitive side effects. We hypothesized that MECT disrupts hippocampal blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, permitting extravasation of peripheral factors that activate microglia, drive synaptic phagocytosis, and precipitate cognitive decline.
METHODS: We employed a multi-modal translational approach integrating: (1) clinical neuroimaging (rs-fMRI and DCE-MRI) and cognitive assessments in 41 MDD patients undergoing MECT (including 9 with DCE-MRI); (2) a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model subjected to electroconvulsive shock (ECS), with behavioral, molecular, and transcriptomic analyses; and (3) causal validation via microglial depletion (PLX5622) and targeted BBB repair (Axitinib). In vitro, HT22 hippocampal neurons were stimulated with soluble inflammatory mediators released by primed microglia to assess direct synaptic injury.
RESULTS: MECT significantly impaired immediate and delayed associative memory and reduced left hippocampal ALFF in MDD patients; memory decline correlated with ALFF reduction. In a paired subgroup of patients, DCE-MRI revealed increased hippocampal Ktrans after MECT, providing preliminary clinical imaging support for treatment-associated BBB hyperpermeability. In CRS mice, ECS downregulated tight junction proteins (Claudin-5, ZO-1, Occludin), induced Evans blue extravasation, and promoted hippocampal deposition of fibrinogen and complement C3. ECS also triggered microglial activation, enhanced PSD95 synaptic phagocytosis, elevated IL-6/IL-1β, and reduced synaptic proteins. Critically, both PLX5622-mediated microglial depletion and Axitinib-mediated BBB repair reversed these pathological changes and rescued cognitive function, establishing a dual causal validation system. Axitinib failed to suppress LPS-induced microglial activation, suggesting its protective effects were mediated via BBB restoration rather than direct immunomodulation.
CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, this study identifies a hippocampus-centered neurovascular-immune mechanism underlying MECT/ECS-related cognitive impairment. Our findings demonstrate that BBB disruption is an early upstream event that permits peripheral factors to enter the brain, activate microglia, and drive synaptic injury and cognitive decline. These results establish a novel mechanistic framework for the cognitive side effects of MECT and highlight BBB protection and microglial modulation as potential strategies for cognitive protection.

articles.title: Therapeutic strategies in vascular cognitive impairment: Insights from the bilateral common carotid artery stenosis mouse model.
articles.abstract: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is a major consequence of cerebrovascular disease, but disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is increasingly recognized not simply as reduced cerebral blood flow, but as a sustained disturbance of oxygen delivery, capillary perfusion, neurovascular coupling, blood-brain barrier integrity, glial homeostasis, white matter maintenance, and synaptic network function. The bilateral common carotid artery stenosis (BCAS) mouse model is a central experimental platform for studying hypoperfusion-related VCI, as it exhibits reproducible cerebral blood flow reduction, white matter pathology, gliovascular injury, and cognitive impairment while permitting genetic manipulation, longitudinal imaging, retinal readouts, omics profiling, and therapeutic testing. This review synthesizes therapeutic studies in BCAS model mice across vascular/endothelial and hemodynamic mechanisms, oxidative and ferroptotic stress, ion-water transport, neuronal excitability and synaptic support, remote ischemic conditioning, regenerative and cell-based approaches, and biomarker-driven model refinement. Across these domains, successful interventions frequently converge on interconnected network nodes rather than isolated linear pathways, linking endothelial function, blood-brain barrier stability, redox-lipid balance, astrocytic ion-water regulation, microglial repair states, oligodendrocyte maturation, myelin integrity, and circuit plasticity. However, methodological heterogeneity concerning surgery, animal characteristics, behavioral testing, treatment timing, and outcome selection restricts translation. Future BCAS studies should prespecify treatment windows, particularly delayed-treatment paradigms initiated after objectively documented hypoperfusion, white matter injury, or cognitive impairment. Studies should also incorporate systemic dose-response assessments, biomarker-guided treatment stratification, clinically relevant comorbidities, and rational combination therapies. Such approaches may convert mechanistic insights from chronic hypoperfusion models into clinically credible therapeutic strategies for VCI.

articles.title: Adhesive cationic hyaluronic acid loading with small extracellular vesicles from IL-6 activated mesenchymal stem cells improves repair of corrosive esophageal injury.
articles.abstract: The treatment of corrosive esophageal injury (CEI) remains challenging due to recurrent courses, frequent complications, and severe tissue damage. Enhancing the therapeutic potential of mesenchymal stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) through cytokine preconditioning has emerged as a promising strategy. In this study, functionally enhanced sEVs (E-sEVs) were generated by pretreating umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells with interleukin-6 (IL-6). E-sEVs exhibited superior capabilities in promoting fibroblast migration and suppressing macrophage-mediated inflammation compared to naïve sEVs. To improve local retention and therapeutic efficacy, E-sEVs were integrated into a cationic hyaluronic acid (CHA) hydrogel with strong bioadhesive properties, forming a composite system termed E-sEVs@CHA. In vitro assays demonstrated that E-sEVs@CHA effectively promoted endothelial cell invasion, exhibited antioxidant activity, and modulated macrophage polarization toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype. In a rat model of CEI, E-sEVs@CHA significantly reduced esophageal inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrotic remodeling, leading to improved tissue repair and reduced stricture formation. This study presents a novel cell-free therapeutic strategy with translational potential for the management of corrosive esophageal injury.

articles.title: Neuroprotective potential of vitamin D3 against glucocorticoid-induced neurotoxicity: Focus on calcium-binding proteins and neuroinflammation in a rat model.
articles.abstract: Prolonged glucocorticoid (GC) therapy is frequently complicated by secondary vitamin D3 deficiency, which acts as a potential pathogenetic modulator of GC-induced neurotoxicity. This study investigated the role of disturbed calcium homeostasis and neuroinflammation in GC-induced brain damage and evaluated the protective potential of vitamin D3 (VD3, cholecalciferol). Female Wistar rats (n = 54) were divided into control, GC-treated (prednisolone, 5 mg/kg/day, 30 days, per os), and VD3-correction (1000 IU/kg/day, concurrent with GC) groups. Analysis of calcium-binding protein levels (calbindin-D28K, S100B, osteocalcin) and neurospecific markers (NF-L, MBP, GFAP) was performed using ELISA, Western blot, and confocal microscopy. Prolonged prednisolone administration caused significant systemic and local 25(OH)D3 deficiency, accompanied by a twofold reduction in osteocalcin protein content and elevated calbindin-D28K levels. Reactive astrogliosis, characterized by increased GFAP+ cell counts and S100B content, occurred alongside decline in NG2+ oligodendrocyte precursors. Significant neuroinflammation was recorded: TNF-α levels rose 1.62-fold in the cortex and 1.65-fold in the hippocampus, while IL-1β increased 2.66-fold and 2.40-fold, respectively. Furthermore, markedly increased serum levels of NF-L, S100B, GFAP, and MBP indicated alterations consistent with blood-brain barrier dysfunction and neuro-glial disintegration. VD3 therapy effectively restored serum markers (osteocalcin, S100B, MBP), suppressed astrocyte reactivity, and normalized cortical cytokine levels while partially replenishing NG2+ cell pool. Although its impact on hippocampal inflammation was limited, these findings demonstrate that maintaining adequate VD3 levels is paramount for preserving CNS integrity by stabilizing calcium buffering and suppressing neuroinflammation. Our results emphasize clinical importance of monitoring VD3 status to mitigate risk of glucocorticoid-induced neurotoxicity and associated neurological complications.

articles.title: Imaging of Vascular Diseases of the Spinal Cord.
articles.abstract: Spinal cord vascular diseases are rare but pose a significant diagnostic challenge and can lead to devastating neurologic injury. Timely diagnosis is challenging given their heterogeneous presentations and overlapping features. This article provides an anatomic framework for understanding spinal vascular pathologies, key imaging patterns, and clinical nuances to improve diagnostic accuracy and guide treatment for a variety of conditions including spinal cord ischemia, spinal vascular malformations, spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas, spinal aneurysms, and cerebrospinal fluid venous fistulas.

articles.title: Vascular and lymphatic dysregulation via non-EndoMT Col2a1 signaling in bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw.
articles.abstract: Bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ) is a severe complication of antiresorptive therapy with poorly understood vascular mechanisms. Here, we integrate whole-organ tissue-clearing imaging, single-cell transcriptomics, and proteomics to construct a multimodal atlas of the mouse and human BRONJ mandibular microenvironment. We identify gross vascular and lymphatic rarefaction and four endothelial subtypes with aberrant Col2a1 upregulation. Fibroblasts and macrophages emerge as key endothelial interactors, highlighting dysregulation of the endothelium-matrix-immune axis. Unlike homeostatic Dmp1⁺/Tfap2a⁺ fibroblasts and Stab1⁺ macrophages, BRONJ lesions feature pathological Lrrc15⁺/Chad⁺ fibroblasts and Il6⁺ macrophages, driving ectopic chondrogenesis and inflammation. Mechanistically, the COL2A1-CD44 axis (EC-to-fibroblast/macrophage signaling) and COL2A1-SDC4 axis (EC-to-fibroblast signaling) are upregulated in BRONJ disease condition, while lineage tracing excludes EndoMT, implicating extracellular matrix remodeling. We functionally validate this axis via localized Col2a1 siRNA silencing and endothelial-specific genetic deletion. Cross-species validation in human mandibles confirms vascular-lymphatic dysregulation, inflammation, and chondrogenesis. Overall, we establish vascular and lymphatic dysregulation as a BRONJ hallmark and identify the COL2A1-CD44/SDC4 axis as a therapeutic target.

articles.title: Endothelial cell-microglia crosstalk mediates heart failure-associated synaptic loss and cognitive impairment in male mice.
articles.abstract: Cognitive impairment affects 30%-80% of patients with heart failure, yet the mechanisms beyond reduced brain blood flow remain poorly defined. Here we show that circulating factors released during heart failure trigger senescence of brain blood-vessel endothelial cells, which in turn drives synaptic loss and cognitive decline through crosstalk between endothelial cells and microglia, the brain's immune cells. Using a pressure-overload model (transverse aortic constriction) combined with plasma transfer in 8-month-old male mice, we found that elevated circulating TGFβ2 acts on endothelial TGFBR2 and induces the secreted protein SPARC via a non-canonical MEK/ERK-MYC pathway. Endothelial SPARC then activates microglial TLR4, promoting neuroinflammation and abnormal engulfment of synapses. Endothelial deletion of Tgfbr2 or Sparc, and microglial deletion of Tlr4, each preserved synapses and improved cognition, and pharmacological Tlr4 inhibition was protective. These findings define an endothelial-microglia signaling axis and a potential therapeutic target in heart failure-associated cognitive impairment.
